Can I not get some definite indication from the minister? He has not told me anything; he has not given any promises-he is extremely careful in that respect. Can I not get some indication that he will make a survey of the situation?

Yes; we will look
into it and if we find towards the end of the year, or well on in the year, that by strict economy we have a little money left over, we shall be more disposed to give heed not only to the representations of my hon. friend but to the other claims to which I referred a few moments ago.

Do I understand from the
minister, then, that if he has a little money left over later in the year he will send a man to investigate?

Surely; and let me make
this observation to the minister while I am on the subject. I think his officials could get a large amount of very useful information from the provincial Department of Agriculture, and the two departments working together ought to be able to show that what I have been trying 'to convince the minister of is absolutely correct.

I can understand the
earnestness with which the hon. member for Fort William made his plea for an experimental farm in the section of the province of Ontario for which he spoke, because I have reason to know the great benefit which the Kapuskasing experimental farm in my part of the country has been to the farmers. Our people are making application for an increase of at least $10,000 in the grant to that farm. We always think of northern Ontario in terms of mining or of lumbering; but it is also a well-known fact that in that part of the province we have one of the finest sections for colonization and for purposes of cultivation. It is well known that the forestry branch in Ontario is spending nearly one million dollars in preventive work to safeguard our forests from the fire danger. And so far as the mining industry is concerned, large sums are being spent in several sections in the way of experimentation. The Kapuskasing farm is doing wonderful work among the settlers, encouraging them in experimenting with new kinds of grain which mature earlier than in other sections of Ontario and Quebec by reason of the fact that the season is shorter. This farm has a total area of 1,270 acres. From this area, about 300 acres are under stump pasture and 650 acres under cultivation. From this last amount over 200 acres are under experimental work and those who know what work is associated with such a large field of experimentation will have an idea of the cost of operation.
The labour conditions in the northern section of northern Ontario are such that we have to pay very high wages. The climatic conditions and the short seasons make it necessary to do the work as rapidly as possible, which in many cases increases the expense.
The appropriation for this station last year was $45,759. It will take, roughly $41,500 for salaries and wages only, leaving less than $5,000 for purchases and improvements. When we take from this amount the cost of supplies and feeding stuffs, it does not leave any for improvements and extension work. However, there is a big need for expansion and
lMr. Motherwell.]
certain improvements. For instance, a better drainage system should be established on parts of the farm, which would increase the yield of crops and facilitate the working of the land. The roads should be fixed so as to facilitate the haulage of crops; better facilities should be arranged to clean the grain for the settlers at cost, and assist them in that way in sowing clean seed; and more purebred live stock and poultry should be kept to enable the settlers to procure foundation stock at reasonable prices. Last year Alaska oats was introduced to the settlers by that farm. This is a variety that is sure to mature in that district, and as it is very satisfactory the demand is so great that they will not be able to supply more than 10 per cent of what is required. This means that it may take several years before the settlers can be supplied with that seed. The demand has been so great that at least fifty thousand bushels could have been sold in this district last year.
Then there is a great deal of land which has been burned over and on which second growth poplar is growing. If we delay this work a few years more it will mean that the cost of clearing this land will be two or three times as great as it would be if the work were done now. If a comparison should be made between the different farms as to the acreage, the climatic conditions, the wages paid and the amount provided by the government it would be seen that this station is not getting its proper share, and I hope the minister will take the matter into consideration as soon as possible.
In 1925 some complaints were made in connection with that farm; a great deal of heavy construction was being done by the Spruce Falls Company at Kapuskasing, and I heard that the experimental farm horses were being used by the company. I made a personal inquiry into the matter and found that the company wanted a certain kind of heavy draft horse which could be supplied only by the experimental farm, so the complaints were not really serious. However, I found also that the superintendent, who is a man well known throughout northern Ontario, a great friend of the northland, appreciated by everyone, a very capable administrator, a man who puts his heart and soul in his work, had to carry an overdraft in his own name amounting to at least $5,000 or $6,000 every year, and I do not think it right that any employee of the government should on his own responsibility be compelled to provide such a large amount of money for governmental work.

Supply-Agriculture-Experimental Farms
I desire to make this plea very earnestly; millions of dollars have been spent in experimental work in connection with mining and forestry, and I am firmly convinced that the house will support an increase of at least $10,000 in the estimates for the farm at Kapuskasing. Just to mention one point which requires consideration, hon. members may be aware that when trees are 'brought up from the southern part of. the province they do not get on very well; they are not adapted to the northern country. I believe there is a good deal of work to be done in that connection, and this could be carried on at the farm. So I hope the Minister of Agriculture will see his way clear to increase the estimate for the Kapuskasing experimental farm by at least $10,000, and I feel confident that if he does he will receive the wholehearted support of the entire representation in the house.

This farm at Kapuskasing was established during the war, largely to demonstrate the agricultural possibilities of that great clay belt along the line of the Canadian National railway. It happens that while this farm is easy of access it is the only farm in the Dominion which I have not visited; I have been so delighted with the look of it from the train that perhaps I have passed it over for that reason. You know, once you get on a railway train you want to get to your destination as quickly as possible, but I think I can promise my hon. friend that I will stop off at this farm sometime during the coming summer, and if circumstances seem to warrant it we will see if we cannot provide more than S46,000 for that work. However, my hon. friend's suggestion that 810,000 is necessary properly to equip that farm is an argument in favour of out general policy of putting the existing farms in better shape before establishing new ones.

Our expenditure on experimental farms seems to increase year by year, but I am not sure that our agricultural industry has been improved in any way. The fact is that we are using up our resources of soil and fertility, and the farmer is not able even to get credit at the bank in order to carry him through his working season. The fact is that the man on the land who is farming in a small way is not able to make it go, and our experimental work does not seem to touch that man or make life easier for him in any way. Unless a man is a capitalist and spends a good deal of money on his farm he cannot make it pay; he must have modem machinery and live stock and everything else in connection with a big farm. The man who is on the land to make his home through his awn efforts is gradually squeezed off, and somehow our experimental farm work does not help him.
This is a condition of affairs which I should like to see remedied. There is no doubt that this morning the leader of the opposition was quite right in his description of agriculture, but the remedy he suggests is quite wrong; he wants a still bigger dose of the poison which has ruined the whole system of agriculture already. We must get closer to the man on the land and allow him to settle there and make his home through his own efforts. It is not a case of providing city conditions for young people on the farms; it is a case of making the farm pay.
How is that to be done? I hope the minister has thought it out. If he possibly can, the farmer will improve his land, but he is up against the big factor of inadequate returns for his labour, and we are forever making more distinct the dividing line between the capitalist and the worker; we are bringing our people to the servitude of wage earners instead of the freedom of home builders. The tenacity of scab mite varies according to different varieties. According to Gerlach, the least resistant are the sarcoptis which die in dry air in a few days.	_	_
The dermatocoptis mites live outside the body from 4 to 6 weeks, but longer in damp and dirty stables, and can remain alive even in dry air for 10 to 14 days.
This is an authoritative statement, and now I want to show how this department handles this situation. In November, 1927, a very high class farmer named Richardson bought an animal at auction which may be described by the following couplet:
The farmer called him Mike, because
That's the kind of a cow he was.
We admit that mange existed on the farm from which the animal was bought, but the government inspectors investigated conditions there, ordered all the cattle dipped, cleaned them all up and certified that it was safe for this farmer to buy "mike".
Mr. Richardson bought the animal and took it to his farm. Three months later, on March 8, this animal was put up for sale at Bowrnan-ville and was purchased by a man living near Peterborough, and eleven months later the government inspectors found that the animal had mange. Then Mr. Richardson, who had sold the animal, prepared his stock for sale; he had worked on his heard for twenty years and it had been regularly inspected by the government inspectors; as a matter of fact they went to this farm thirteen times in one year, 1928, and examined these animals, and gave a certificate to the effect that Mr. Richardson had an accredited herd. However, after these thirteen visits, another inspector discovered that this animal Mike at Peterborough hod mange. Just when Mr. Richardson has his herd' ready to sell, and after he had paid $10 a head to have them included in the sale, the inspector came along and notified him that the cattle were not to be placed on the block, and he advertised that fact all over the country. Then he inspected the premises and the entire herd; unable to find any trace of mange on any animal, he then issued a certificate saying that this action had been taken on "suspicion"; he only suspected that something was wrong with this herd.
The situation was so critical and so unbelievable that I engaged a high class veterinary
Supply-Agriculture

and took him to this farm, where he and I examined every animal. This veterinary gave me the following certificate:
March 5th, 1929.
This is to certify that this day, at the request of Dr. Kaiser, member of parliament for Ontario riding, I made a special inspection of the premises and entire herd of cattle owned by L. Richardson and Son of Ashburn, township of Whitby, and herein state that in no case could be found a visible sign of mange, past or present, in any animal of the whole herd; and furthermore, as a veterinary, I have visited the stock for many years past, and I have never seen any skin affection which even suggested mange, upon any animal upon the farm.
W. A. MacNeely, V.S.,
Brooklin, Ontario.
This farmer had gone to considerable trouble and had built up a magnificent herd but on account of this interference on the part of the department he was deprived of the only chance he had to cash in. He could not put these cattle up as high grade stock and receive up to $300 per head for them, but was obliged to take them from the block and sell them on the market as ordinary animals. I saw one of these animals myself; it looked to be absolutely perfect, and a stockman assured me that it was easily worth $500. Instead of accomplishing something of value to stockmen these officials are actually doing damage not only to this man's herd, but to other herds in the same neighbourhood. The British and European authorities claim that mange cannot exist beyond three months, even under the most favourable circumstances. During the last fifteen or twenty years it has been proved that there are periods of incubation beyond which there is no danger. It might as well be said that a man should not risk catching smallpox by going to the home of another man who had it three years ago, as to say that an animal can catch the mange after eleven or twelve months. The government has enacted certain regulations which appear to me in some respects to be as old as, or perhaps older, than the Minister of Agriculture. Let any sensible man consider these regulations and see what conclusion he can arrive at from such a regulation as this:
No animal which is affected or has been exposed to the infection of mange shall be permitted to run at large or come in contact with any animal not so affected or exposed.
This does not recognize the period of incubation or make any time allowance for quarantine, but if such an animal comes in contact with another animal then the department may step in at any time and destroy the results of efforts extending over twenty-
five or thirty years. If the minister should conclude that what I am saying is the truth, then this government should compensate that farmer for the loss which he has sustained. He has suffered not only a loss in the value oif his cattle, but also a loss in prestige. I ask the government to investigate this case, and if I am correct in my statements then the minister should call off some of these half educated veterinary surgeons and place in charge of this work sensible men who understand something of the evolution of disease.

The officers of the department put a quarantine on these animals and said that they were unsafe to be sent out to a sale. There is no doubt that an animal can carry mange for as long as two years and show no visible signs of it.
Where does the minister get that authority?

Anyone who knows anything about what is called burrowing mange knows that it can be carried that length of time. Surface mange- is easily diagnosed, 'but the experience with this burrowing mange has shown that i-t may be carried at least two years without being diagnosed. Our records show that a veterinary practitioner reported mange on the premises of Mr. Melville Pinnett, of Indian River, Ontario, and scrapings taken by Inspector Gihson- from a 'bull in Pinnett's herd were examined in our laboratory and sarcoptes found. These are the burrowing mites and this mange is difficult to cure. The following is a memorandum regarding this outbreak at Indian River:
The disease was probably introduced into the herd of Mr. Melville Pinnett, of Indian River, Ont., by a bull purchased at a Bowman-ville sale in March, 1928, and originally coming from the herd of James Compton, of Ashburn, Ont.
Mr. Compton's premises were quarantined for sarcoptic mange in the fall of 1926 and released in March, 1927, after the cattle had been treated three times, but this bull probably carried infection in spite of treatments.
The outbreak on Mr. Compton's premises was apparently introduced through a cow purchased from Mr. John Miller of Ashburn, Ont., and which had been purchased by the latter in Alberta some five years previously. This animal had shown skin trouble at the time of purchase by Mr. Miller but had subsequently apparently recovered.
Further evidence that sarcoptic mange was present in Mr. Miller's herd before 1924, probably brought in by western cattle, is found in the fact that a number of cattle imported by Messrs. Dryden and Miller from Scotland in 1924 and subsequently sold in 1925 were found to be infected. It is unlikely that the infection

Supply-A griculture
was introduced by the imported cattle since these were inspected by a Canadian veterinary officer in Scotland and kept under continual observation during the quarantine period at Quebec, and no clinical symptoms noted.
The hon. member is complaining that we did not allow these susipected animals to go to this sale and thus be distributed to the four corners of Ontario. In order to safeguard our live stock it is necessary to take every precaution to see that such animals are not let loose at a sale. There is no question that it is a hardship, but in the public interests of the community it is necessary that these precautionary measures be taken. They are carried out on the advice of the very best veterinary surgeons we can obtain, and it is regrettable that these hardships must prevail with respect to the individual. You cannot take a chance with any of these diseases. It has been found necessary to impose regulations as to shipments of merchandise, et cetera, with regard to the foot and mouth disease, and although they may seem very harsh it is necessary to take every precaution to keep out any of these infectious diseases. Safety first must be our policy, especially when action is being taken under the advice of one of our competent authorities. I am very sorry for the gentleman who apparently suffered loss by reason of not being able to submit his cattle at the sale. I understand from my deputy-I did not catch it from my hon. friend-that this man, by reason of not being able to submit these animals at the sale, lost the sale of them and that he wants compensation. The law makes no such provision and therefore I am unable to give the matter favourable consideration. We give compensation for animals slaughtered 'or bovine tuberculosis, but not for cases of this kind.

The minister misunderstands me altogether. I do not complain because this man was shut off from the sale. What I complain of is this, that when he bought this animal the government certified that it was right; that it was clean; that it would not scatter the disease. The animal was observed for sixty days and then the man was assured that it was all right. Of what benefit is this government certificate? A man in good faith accepted it; he built up his herd and then when he expected to make a few dollars, he was told that he could not cash in.

There is no system of governmental or other inspection that is 100 per cent correct. This kind of mange does not show at times. It is a burrowing mange
that is beyond the ken of the ordinary eye. At certain periods of the year it will develop and manifest itself, but it may be carried for at least two years and in the interim a clean certificate may be given. Otherwise it might have to be quarantined still further. When there is a reasonable presumption that there is no danger of mange, the quarantine is removed and the certificate is given. If the inspector had taken absolutely no chance for that period of two years, there would have been all the greater howl because we kept the animal in quarantine for so long. We took a chance in liberating it and eventually it developed that it had the mange of this description. Then the gentleman, not being able to sell it, no doubt suffered loss. We have had placed before us a number of claims for compensation of that nature, but before we could deal with them, the law would have to be amended. The question whether we shall widen the scope of the law as regards compensation is a matter for consideration. The act has not been up for revision for some years and I should be glad to consider the question of widening its scope. But if the door is opened for compensation for that disease, it will have to be opened for some others and we shall have claims for all kinds of cases similar to the one which my hon. friend has mentioned.

I think the trouble with the department is that having the life history of this burrowing mange, they did not act as they should have done. As soon as mange is discovered amongst animals on a farm, they should prevent the sale of them. The trouble arose when the department permitted the animal to be sold in the first instance. Having the life history of the burrowing mange as the department has it, that it may remain concealed for two years, I cannot understand how any veterinary officer would release an animal for sale within that period and take chances of the disease being distributed to other farms. The criticism would lie there rather than in the permission to allow the second sale. If the department is satisfied as to its diagnosis that this burrowing mange may exist for two years-and I agree with them in that so far as mange goes-^they should issue regulations providing that no sale may take place from a farm where such mange has been found.
I want to bring a different case of quarantine to the attention of the minister and I do not think he can find any regulations whereby he can escape responsibility. I brought to his attention a farm where a quarantine
Private Bills

had been established some four months previously in a case of suspected rabies. A man had lost several cattle and also a dog had been acting suspiciously. A quarantine had been established. Following that a biological examination, I have no doubt, was made, and the possibility of rabies was disproved, negatived. But notwiththstanding that, this man was allowed to continue for four months with that quarantine on his farm. I have a letter under my hand and if the deputy will kindly wait, he can get all the details. I am not going to say that the greatest precaution should not be taken in the matter of quarantine. That is one action which you must take in preventing the spread of disease. But in this case what happened is that I verily believe the inspector forgot all about his quarantine and that farm was quarantined from May to September, although, as I say, a pathological examination had been made and the result was negative as regards rabies. The inspector should have gone back to that farm. He comes back and says: "Oh, I permitted him to sell farm produce." The farmer did not understand that and I could not get the quarantine placard because the inspector came out, grabbed it and took it away. I should like to see that quarantine placard. Why was he so keen to grab it and take it away when his attention was drawn to the length of the quarantine? That farmer was left there for four months under quarantine without any reason whatever and he had reached almost a destitute condition before the attention of the department was called to the matter. Then the inspector rushed up, removed the placard and said: "Everything is fine, but we think we were justified in our quarantine."

Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey): Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to the third reading of this bill on the ground that evidence was improperly admitted, and once this evidence was admitted the co-respondent was not given sufficient time to face the charges that were made. Procedure Respecting Divorce
reading of the bill. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth):
That the said bill be not now read a third time, but that it be sent back to the select standing committee on private bills with instructions that they have power to make further investigation.

I was not present last night when this bill was being considered in committee, but I have read what took place. It seems to me that in spite of the apparent desire of the house to vote all these bills through without any regard to the merits of each case or to the evidence brought or not brought in connection therewith, there should be at least some semblance of decency. I appeal to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I do not know this case, and I am simply taking the declarations as they were made last night in the house. It was stated last night by two hon. members that this divorce was being granted on a charge the witness to which was a perjurer-at least the evidence of his perjury was quite clear; that the proof made by the police agent was entirely unsound. He stated that the respondent and another party stopped at a certain hotel under a certain name. Now the person to Whom that name belongs states that he lived at that place with his wife. Therefore this is a dear case, if not of perjury, of gross mistake. Application was made for a new hearing, and it was refused because of lack of time. The position seems to have been taken generally in this house that the whole responsibility rests with the committee of the Senate, but surely what we are doing here must count for something. Quebec dlaims to be opposed to the establishment of divorce courts on principle and believes that it is better to keep the present system because it offers a guarantee of careful scrutiny and is in effect a law instead of a judgment. But in a case like this if the statements, corroborated yesterday by the member for Brant (Mr. Smoke) and the member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan), are accurate, our decision may be in the form of a law, but we shall make it in defiance of the most elementary principles of justice and equity. We shall be ratifying blindly not a judgment but a decision by another body forming part of this parliament. For my part I protest once more most emphatically and most unequivocally against this manner of dissolving marriages. It is against
all principles of morality, it is against all principles of law, it is against all principles of evidence, it is against all principles which are supposed to be upheld by parliaments and courts of justice. I refuse to be a party responsible for any such miscarriage of justice.

I am informed that the Senate committee was not by any means a unit in this matter, though of that I have not any information in the report itself. But we have in this case as in many others evidence given by certain detectives. Their work is 'being recognize as a greater outrage than anyone could have imagined before we started discussing divorce bills this session. I am informed that one detective with his accomplice-if I may use that term, and I think it is proper here-has been responsible for securing evidence in some fifty cases, and that in some instances he has resorted to the most abominable practices in order to secure that evidence. These professional detectives try to lure their victims into vice and then turn round and report the evidence thus framed up in order that they may secure sufficient grounds on which to obtain a divorce. I say it is an abominable practice, and I cannot think that the conscience of this country will tolerate very much longer the practice of relying on evidence coming from such a source.
With regard to this particular case, it is quite obvious that somebody is committing perjury. I am not sure who it is. Will the ministei be kind enough to make a statement in connection with what he has done to carry out the resolution of the house at last session:
That in the opinion of this house, in order to test and demonstrate the possibilities of pulverized coal, the government should adapt one of their steamers on the Pacific coast, and the furnace of one of the government public buildings in British Columbia, to the use of pulverized coal from Vancouver island mines.
I have been taking this matter up with the government from time to time. At first there was delay owing to the fact that the department was observing the result of the experiment on the Lingan which had been equipped by the British Steel Corporation to use pulverized coal. This delayed the government's plans quite a while, because they

Supply-Mines and Geological Survey
thought they might as well benefit by that experiment. After a prolonged trial it appeared to have been a total failure. This must have been due to some defect either in the system adapted or in its installation, because I have in my hand the record of an experiment on the New Zealand Shipping Company's steamship Hororata, of 11,200 tons gross, which arrived in New Zealand after a voyage of 11,000 miles from the old country. Half of her boilers were equipped for the use of pulverized coal. It was a very thorough and successful experiment. I see they used all sorts of coal-Welsh steam coal, North of England coal, Scottish coal, Virginian coal, and some New River coal which they obtained at Panama. On the homeward voyage they were going to burn New Zealand coal.
As regards adapting the furnace of one of the government public buildings in British Columbia to use pulverized coal, while the resolution called for that to be done one must not be unreasonable. I have been informed that the only buildings that could be suitably equipped in that way would require a boiler having a rating of 300 horse-power or over, and that there are only two public buildings in Canada that could make use of a heating apparatus of that size. Therefore we cannot expect the experiment to be carried out in British Columbia. But it has been ascertained almost beyond doubt that pulverized coal can be successfully used on land. Several factories have been equipped with apparatus for this purpose, and the system is beyond the experimental stage. But apparently there are vast differences between the conditions governing the installation of the system on land and on the sea; why I do not know. Some people put it down to the Scotch marine boiler, which they claim is not adapted for the use of pulverized coal, and that the tubular boiler should be used. To solve such and other problems is why this house endorsed the idea that the government should experiment on some of the boats of the Canadian government. The British government has done a great deal of research in that way, but it is not entirely useful to us on the Pacific coast, because it appears that the coal from each mine requires special adjustment of the equipment to handle it, and that is why it was thought advisable that we should experiment with our own coal on one of our government boats on the Pacific coast. We are disappointed to find that the Canadian government merchant marine has ordered two
boats to be equipped for oil burning. That is against the spirit and the letter of the resolution of this house.
I find in a report I have here that the Blue Star line-a British line of course-operating a fleet of twenty-six vessels, proposes at the earliest possible moment to equip its fleet with the Clarke Chapman pulverizec fuel system. A recently ordered 9,000 tonne; will be equipped to burn pulverized fuel bj the Brand system. The P. & 0. Steam Navigating Company-one of the biggest in the world-have decided to convert several of their steamers to the Bauer-Wach system of exhaust steam turbine propulsion in combination with pulverized fuel plants. There has been a company formed in England known as the Howden-Buell Combustion Company, Limited, to develop and exploit both marine and land pulverized fuel installations. It was that system which was used on the Hororata which I mentioned at the outset of my remarks. It is apparent that pulverized coal can be utilized. There is needed only a little more enterprise on the part of the government to make it a success.
Hear, hear.

I suggested they should adapt one of the fishery patrol boats on the Pacific, but it is objected that they are too small to justify the installation of the system. This would cost some $15,000 to $20,000 whether the boat be large or small, and we do not want the experiment to be made in such a way that it would be abortive and give a black, eye to the proposal.
I should like the minister to give the committee a statement of what he has done along these lines, and what we may hope he will do to carry out this resolution in the future.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member
for Comox-Albemi has dealt fairly thoroughly with the pulverized fuel situation, and undoubtedly he is keeping very closely in touch with the experiments that are being carried on. We have discovered two or three things in this connection. One is that there must be a laboratory test of the fuel before it is attempted to use it for pulverized fuel firing. Another is that the installation of the mechanical devices for the purpose of using pulverized fuel is very expensive. A third is that so far there have been no successful tests made of boilers under 150 horsepower, which is a fairly large boiler. In the Lingan test on the St. Lawrence from Sydney to Montreal, spoken of by my hon. friend,

Supply-Mines and Geological Survey
I think a mistake was made in equipping all the boilers with pulverized fuel apparatus. When the mechanical device went wrong of course the ship was laid up. We watched the experiment very closely. Had they equipped one half of the boilers, then the ship would have been able to keep going. That was the practice followed in most of the cases where attempts were made on British liners going to New Zealand and later by the shipping company mentioned by my hon. friend.
' My attention was first directed to the advisability of giving serious consideration to pulverized fuel owing to the statement made to me two years ago by the marine engineers located alt tihe British fuel research station that if a complete mechanical system could be devised for this purpose pulverized coal would be a cheaper steam producer than fuel oil which is so rapidly taking the place of coal on ocean going vessels. I made some inquiries at the British fuel research station and found they were experimenting along those lines. I asked them to keep us closely in touch with the results of their experiments. In moat oases where the experiment has been a success they have not equipped the entire ship with pulverized fuel burners. I think it is safe to say that the experiments have been successful and have reduced to a considerable degree the cost of raising steam on these vessels. With respect to our own situation, last year when my hon. friend's motion was being considered I felt it would be possible to install this equipment on some of our lighter craft on the west coast; but after some investigation we deemed it unwise to ask for an experiment on a vessel of tihe size of the one in the fisheries trade on the coast. With respect to what my hon. friend has said regarding stationary plants, we found them too small for our purposes there. I believe there are very great possibilities in connection with pulverized fuel firing for the raising of steam, but so far the mechanical plant costs a considerable amount of money and we have the full advantage of the experiments earned on by British shipping as well as the attempt made on the St. Lawrence in firing on the Lingan. I am now endeavouring to see whether it is not possible to have the merchant marine make an experiment on one of their ships. I do not think it would be wise on the part of the government to spend a large sum of money only to find that the equipment was faulty. In the experimental stage we are severely criticized for spending money; and as in the case of low .temperature carbonization of fuels, in connection with which so much has been done in Great Britain, I thought it 
would be wise for us to wait until we had available sufficient knowledge as to what had been discovered by the experiments carried on in this respect in Great Britain by private companies. I do think, however, that the equipment of one or two boilers in the merchant marine, burning our own fuel from our own Canadian coal, would be worth while; and with that end in view I shall see whether a further experiment cannot be undertaken on our own behalf with respect to pulverized fuel.

The
minister mentioned something about the low carbonization of fuel. What progress has been made since the last session of parliament in connection with testing fuels in western Canada from the standpoint of the low carbonization problem?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have
collected samples from a good many mines in the west. We are establishing now a fairly large plant for testing purposes in the fuel laboratories on Booth dtreet, and as soon as the equipment is in place we shall test fuels by the low carbonization process.

The minister has referred to the importance of small coal; he says he has not thought it desirable to do any experimental work in this regard. The trouble I find with his whole department is that they have never done any real experimental work; what they have done is, in the main, to copy the work of established plants which have demonstrated certain lines of action, and then play 'in a childish way with the same thing themselves. I find that in some of the reports made by the department there are put forward, in regard to the investigation of fuels, statements which I do not consider correct, while others are trivialities. Take for instance one of the publications of the department issued in 1926 in reference to fuels and fuel 'testing. It is said to be a general review of a.n investigation carried out by two gentlemen of the staff, Mr. Haanel and Mr. Gilmore. I will deal briefly with a few of the statements made by these gentlemen. At page 35 of the report they have something to say with respect to the nature of sulphur in cokes made from Canadian coal, and they discuss the experiment they made in connection with a mixture of Nova Scotia and United States ooall. Now I ask the minister this question: Why waste any time on an experiment of that- kind, namely, the coking of a mixture of Nova Sootia and United States coal? What good result will fol-

Supply-Mines and Geological Survey
low therefrom? Will the minister tell me that? I can understand his carrying on experiments with Nova Scotia coal so far as ooke is concerned, although experience in its use dates back fifty or sixty years:	Nova
Scotia coal was coked successfully and used to a considerable extent in Nova Scotia before the minister was born, and, as everybody knows, is still used there. Page after page of this report which I hold in my hand is taken up with experiments carried on by the officers of the minister's department- experiments which mean practically nothing. Here for example is a statement appearing on page 36 of the report:
The coke made from the Sptinghill coal is the only one with a sufficiently low sulphur content to be classed as metallurgical, though the sulphur in the Sydney-Pocohontas, Comox, and Sydney cokes is not much too high.
That statement is absolutely false: thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of tons of pig iron have been made in Nova Scotia with coke solely the product of
the coal mines of Pictou and of Cape Breton and Nova Sootiia. Of that there is no possible doubt. Why then say that coall made from SpringhiH coal is the only one produced in Nova Solatia with a sufficiently low sulphur content bo be classed as metallurgical fuel? The statement, I say, is absolutely untrue, is moat misleading, and is most unfair. In the next paragraph on the same page the writer deals with different farms of sulphur in ooai and coke and makes statements which would be Challenged by anyone with a practical knowledge of the matter. Further down the page he states:
The writer's earlier paper indicates that, in his opinion, while oxidation of the carbonaceous material in coal is the principal cause of spontaneous combustion, the oxidation of finely disseminated pyrites is also a contributing factor.
Of course it is a contributing factor; that is known to everyone who has handled coal and has been known from time immemorial.
Why therefore go into that matter now?
They must print something; that is all.

Take page 43:
Typical western Canadian coals were analysed for sulphate, pyritic and organic sulphur, and the following conclusions drawn:
None of the coking coals from the Mountain park or the two Crowsnest pass areas contain any appreciable amount of pyritic sulphur, nor do the partly coking coals from the Nanaimo area contain much of this form of sulphur. The sample of coking coal from the Comox area contained considerable pyritic sulphur, hut this would be reduced by washing.
Of course it would be reduced by washing; all coals that contain pyrite-and most of 78594-227
them do-can eliminate the sulphur to workable proportions by that method. Coal is washed in Nova Scotia and in other places for two reasons, first to reduce the sulphur and then to reduce the ash; both can be largdly eliminated by successful washing. Here is another gem:
Cokes made from maritime provinces coal, either alone or blended with United States coals, and one coke made from Comox, B.C., coal, were analyzed for sulphide, sulphate, free and solid solution sulphur. It was found that:-
The coke made from SpringhiH coal was the only one with a low enough sulphur content to be classed as a good metallurgical coke.
That is the second time such a statement is made in this report, and it is not a true statement of fact. Then the report goes on:
The cokes made from the Sydney (unwashed) and Comox (washed) coals contained a little too much sulphur to be classed as satisfactory metallurgical cokes.	.
The cokes made from Minto coal contained such a large percentage of sulphur as to render them unsatisfactory for almost any purpose whatever. However, coal washing, _ which would be necessary on account of the high percentage of ash, would greatly reduce the sulphur content.
No one in the maritimes with any sense ever suggested coking Minto coal, because the percentage of sulphur is much too high. It could be washed out, but you would wash out at the same time eight or nine per cent of the total volume of coal, and the ash is also too high; in short it is not a suitable coal. These same arguments apply to other coalls, but to state that maritime province coal generally will not produce good metallurgical fuel is to make a statement which is absolutely untrue. Then on page 44 I find the following:
Considerable variations in the specific gravities of the separating solutions did not to any extent affect the division of pyritic sulphur.
There you are dealing with laboratory experiments instead of ordinary commercial washing; you are dealing with methods of treating coal with solutions of different densities at different strengths. That is only a matter for laboratory experiment. What is the use of continuing that sort of thing and spending tens of thousands of dollars to demonstrate something which was demonstrated thirty or forty years ago in a practical way? I do not say that the present steel and coal companies know all there is to be known with regard to their own coal, but they know more than anyone else knows and they have acquired that knowledge through a long period of years in the daily operations of their plants.
Then on page 47 I find a table dealing with cokes made from Sydney, Sydney-Pocohontas,

Springhill, Minto-Elfchom-Pocohontas and Cotnox coal. There we find the total sulphur, sulphide, sulphate, free sulphur, solid solution sulphur and ash, but all that information was known long ago by the people interested in this coal, that is, the people who consume large quantities of coal in the manufacture of iron and steel in Nova Scotia and Ontario. On page 61 I find the following:
As a general rule "mine" samples contain less ash and have higher calorific values than the corresponding "commercial" samples. .	.
It should also be realized that, generally speaking "slack" coal will contain more moisture and ash and have a lower calorific value than the corresponding screened coal, and that "run-of-mine" coal will be intermediate between the two.
Of course that is so, and any coal miner or coal dealer knows it is so. Why burden a report with material of that kind? It is making this department a laughing stock with people who know anything about this business.
I might proceed to deal with similar matters contained in the report of the Dominion Fuel Board for 1923-28. At page 33 of their report they deal with the low temperature carbonization of bituminous coal, and I want to point out again that Pictou coal has been coked for over sixty years and washed for over forty years. This coal has been coked in beehive ovens for more than three-score years and for one equal period has been used in blast furnace operations. The first rectangular coke ovens on this continent were operated in Pictou county in 1891, and the first commercial coal washer constructed on this continent was operated at the same place in the same year. Half a dozen coal washing plants have been constructed in Pictou county and in Cape Breton since that time, yet here we are given a lot of information which may be of interest to school children but which is of no use to people in the trade. I suggest the minister would be well advised to withdraw a good deal of this information, and I believe his department would stand higher in public estimation if that action were taken.
I might go on and refer to many other matters in connection with these various reports, but I do not think I should take the necessary time. For example, these reports deal with the absorption of moisture, with the depreciation in peat through (handling and many other things of that character which are not of any great value to this or any other country. Most of the material contained in these various reports, of which there are half a dozen, is out of date and has been out of date for years.
My quarrel with the department is that to a very large extent the experiments which [Mr. Cantley.l
have been carried on are simply play boy work based on information which was acquired long ago by people in the business. Practically all the information contained in these reports could have been obtained by simply visiting one of several of the plants in Nova Scotia and taking notes on what has been done by the Old method of trial and error, the only method by which progress is made.
Now I take up the final report of the peat committee, in which reference is made to an attempt to carbonize peat from the Alfred bog. The approximate analysis is given, as follows:
Moisture, 25.6 per cent.
Ash, 4.6 per cent.
Volatile matter, 48 per cent.
Fixed carbon, 21.3 per cent.
Calorific valuer, B.T.U's, 7,040.
This calorific value is just about half that of really good Nova Scotia coal. An experiment was carried on in connection with the carbonization of this peat, and one very peculiar thing in connection with that experiment is that the fuel used to heat the ovens was 2,654 pounds of slack coal. Why did you not use peat; why use slack coal? You are attempting to carbonize peat; is there not sufficient heat units in the peat to warm up the ovens in order to carry out the carbonization? Could anything be more ridiculous than a performance of that kind? There are many like cases which I could mention, but I do not want to take up any more time of the committee. This department has carried on experimental work for more than twenty years at a cost of hundreds of thousands of dollars and the results have been one continuous failure, especially with regard to the experiments carried on with peat. There has been duplication in the securing of information concerning subjects which have long ago been investigated by private enterprises unassisted by government aids and depending wholly upon the commercial results obtained. In other words, knowledge has been gained by the old method by which all useful' information has been acquired. I submit that the time has oomie when this waste of the public money should be stopped, and I hope the minister will stop it.
I would like to compare the work done by the mines department with that which has been carried on in Great Britain and on the continent. And here may I say I have nothing but praise for the other department under the minister's management, the geological survey, but I can find very little to praise and much to condemn in the work carried on by the mines department. As the result of the war Germany lost a large proportion of the territory which has previously supplied her

Supply-Mines and Geological Survey
with a great deal of her bituminous coal; I refer to Silesia, which was awarded to Poland. How did she meet that situation? By utilizing what they call brown coal, which is practically the same as our lignite, and to-day we find her using that coal, formerly neglected, in her open hearth gas producers, using it to run her steel and iron works, and as the fuel for the carrying on of other industries. Prior to the wiar they had not dreamed of being able to do tihis work with their lignite. If the department desires to learn how to deal with the lignite in the western provinces they should send someone to Germany to see how she is solving that problem. It would not cost anything to get that information, outside of sending a really capable man there.
Enormous progress has been made in the use of powdered coal, as was referred to by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). Probably the greatest problem in the use of this fuel is the upkeep of the pulverizing machinery, because that machinery wears out faster than any other known type of machine. Statements have been made in some of these publications that pulverized coal can be stored, can be carried in tubes, can be blown into furnaces, and the same things are said with regard' to pulverized peat, such statements are not correct. If such is attempted you will have explosions, because coal in a pulverized condition is highly explosive and when a certain proportion of aiir is mixed with the coal a spark or even friction will set it off. Anyone who has seen the results of dust explosions in any of our collieries will have some knowledge of the tremendously destructive effect of coal dust explosions. We in Nova Scotia have had for years experience in firing heating furnaces and reheating furnaces with pulverized coal. We at first had the idea that it could be stored in bins, conveyed through pipes and blown into furnaces, but we found that that was impracticable. It collects moisture very rapidly and then cakes up, and there are other reasons which I need not refer to.
Is the minister aware that internal combustion engines are to-day being operated in Germany with pulverized coal in the same manner in which petrol or gasoline is used? The advances made in connection- with the use of pulverized fuel in Great Britain have been very great. The minister has said that the boilers which were here available for experimentation by him were too small as they were only 150 horse-power. How many horsepower, may I ask him, is there available in the hearting plant in connection with this building? When a new installation of boilers was being -asked for last year I suggested to the Minister of Public Works thia/t the boilers 78594-227i
be fitted up to use pulverized fuel., If that had been done a demonstration plant would have been provided and the men of the department could have watched the results of the operation, every day. Why was not advantage taken of that opportunity? I would like the minister to answer that question.

speechtext: I thought the hon. member was making a speech and I did not want to interrupt him; I intended to answer him when he had finished.

The minister has indulged in some talk at times, more particularly when he returned last year from the other side of the Atlantic, regarding the by-products which could be obtained from coal in the form of oil. The latest information which is available in connection with thart is to the effect that under existing conditions this process is unprofitable with the use of high temperature distillation and that the profits to be derived from low temperature carbonization are even more problematical. So far my remarks have been what the minister might term destructive, but I do not want to stop there. I would like to make one recommendation to the minister, and E would be very glad if he would adopt it. It. is this: instead of spending time and money in carrying out experiments with regard to things which have been well known, determined and settled long ago, take two or three of the brightest men from his department and send them to the old country, to Germany, to -the United States and to France to observe and study what other people are doing in a commercial and practical way. If that were done the minister would be able to give us some information -which would be of en-ormous value to -the industries of this country. These books issued from his department may have some value to the primary schools, but are of no value to the industries of this country, whether coal mining, coke producing, iron or steel making, or any of the kindred -industries.

Mr. Chairman, 1 do not intend to go in-to the in-tricacies of the analyses of -the different grades of coal which the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) has suggested that the government should further investigate, but one thing which is obvious to all the people of Canada is that no serious -attempt has been made- to develop a national fuel- policy. We have a national fuel board costing this country about-$20,000 a year. They submit reports to par-

liament, and certain investigations are carried on by 'them with respect to analyses and other matters of a highly technical and intricate character, but we are left completely in the dark with regard to the general -basis of developing a national fuel policy, which is one of the most important matters that the country could deal with. If the expense involved to carry on the fuel board, namely, $20,000, is not sufficient to broaden their scope, I would suggest to the minister that enough money be placed at their disposal to enable them at least to carry on an investigation with respect to the development of a national fuel policy for the Dominion. Such a move would prove of benefit not only to the eastern portion but also to the midwest and the extreme western portions of the Dominion. I offer this suggestion to the minister in all seriousness and I hope before long some properly constituted agency of the government, it matters little whether it be the fuel board or some other commission, will develop and inaugurate a national fuel policy for the Dominion so that we may use the great resources we have instead of importing such huge quantities of fuel from foreign countries.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman, the minister is aware that the fuel question in central Canada is an outstanding one. We are vitally interested in procuring a supply of fuel from purely Canadian sources. In fact we are prepared to use the soft coal of the east and the soft and hard coal of the west for domestic purposes simply to maintain a market for Canadian coal. It is true the bulk of domestic coal used in Ontario and Quebec is imported from the United States. The people of these two central provinces
feel that we should be self-contained so far as our fuel supply is concerned. Viewed from the economic and every other standpoint, from which source would the Minister of Mines advise the people of Ontario and Quebec to procure their coal, from Alberta, from Nova Scotia, or from the United States?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I certainly would advise them to procure it from Alberta and eastern Canada; that would be my first choice. But on the other hand it must be borne in mind that in order to protect the manufacturing interests of central Canada we must get them their fuel somewhere within reasonable reach of the prices at which they can procure it across the line. That is what we have been endeavouring to do.

I thank the minister for his answer. I feel I am speaking the mind of the great bulk of the people of the central provinces when I say we are prepared to make many sacrifices to secure a supply of coal from our own mines. In this connection I would say that, if necessary, the freight rates on coal should be cut down to a minimum so that we might be able to secure our supply within our own borders.

What efforts have the department made.-outside of those that the minister has mentioned with respect to lower freight rates-to develop in Canada a national fuel policy? If such a policy means anything it must mean an attempt to use as much of our own coal as possible. I cannot see that there has been any concerted effort on the part of the department, outside of reductions in freight rates, to develop a fuel policy for this country. I would ask the minister to enlarge on that point, because it is of very serious interest and concern to the people of the maritime provinces.

I think that is only fair. I have asked the minister a question and I am entitled to an answer. The fuel board as at present constituted is not able to cope with the problem; it has not the resources to enable it to carry on investigations. It is therefore the duty of parliament to give the board wider scope and more money to enable it to evolve for Canada a fuel policy which will be beneficial to this country. To-day we are simply drifting so far as fuel consumption is concerned-drifting towards importations from foreign countries, mostly from the United States. I would like to know also what has been done in connection with the control of the waste gases in the Turner valley. As the minister knows, this question was up last year; it has been discussed from time to time and it is a matter of some importance.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I was in Calgary recently, 'but was unable to visit the Turner valley field. However, we do know that a very large quantity of gas is escaping at that field, and the provincial government and our own officials have become somewhat concerned about the wastage. We have agreed to appoint a joint commission to investigate the matter and, if possible, suggest methods for its conservation or use. A great many suggestions have been made in this connection, but before taking any definite steps we thought it well to have a thorough investigation made. Doctor Camsell is chairman of the board which has been created for that purpose, the other members being Mr. Ross, our mining engineer, and Mr. Carpenter of the utilities board of the province of Alberta. At the moment I think they are beginning their work and I expect a report in a short time.

I am glad some action has been taken, because while possibly a large number of people throughout the country and perhaps many members of this house do not know it, I am sure the minister is aware of the fact that the supply of gas is not unlimited and that a field can be drained as readily as a country can be deforested.

That is the point I had in mind, because we all know it can be extracted successfully; it is purely a matter of how much it costs, and I was directing my inquiry along that line.

Anyone who has paid any attention to this coal question must realize the difficulties confronting coal producers in Canada. I appreciate the difficulties which face the minister, but I do not think he is proceeding as he should. I quite appreciate the position we are in, with the coal fields of the United States so close to the industrial centres of Canada, which makes it possible for these industrial concerns to get American coal quite cheaply; there is no doubt that we will have a great deal of difficulty in meeting that competition. That is a question of transportation, and the minister appears to devote the most of his attention to that question. But transportation is only one element which has to be considered; there are many other and probably just as important factors in connection with this problem. There is the element of the cost of production; then there is the element of transportation; then comes the element of marketing, and, last but not
least, the element of competition. When I had the honour of addressing this house upon this question I pointed out what I thought was a feasible plan, one which might afford some solution of the problem and cause the government to give some consideration to the formulating of a national fuel policy. We admit that under ordinary circumstances it is impossible to put Nova Scotia or Alberta coal into central Canada to compete on an even footing with American coal; that may as well be admitted first as last. But as the hon. member for South Renfrew said a few moments ago, the people of Ontario and western Quebec are willing to make a sacrifice in order that we may become independent, as far as fuel resources are concerned. Of course everyone must realize that there is a limit to the extent to which the good people of Ontario would be prepared to go in that direction. The suggestion which I offered last year was the appointment of a commission to investigate the cost of production, the cost of transportation, the cost of marketing, and last but not least, the element of protection, but I am afraid that in that connection we will not have the sympathy of the present Minister of Finance. It was stated this afternoon that the present Minister of Mines rather prided himself on the quotation with reference to the "death knell of protection." Additional protection is needed on our coal in order that it may successfully invade the markets of central Canada. The government deserves credit for giving us a three dollar rate on coal to points in Quebec, but that is not enough. This national fuel policy will never be evolved by considering only one element. I suggest that a commission of outstanding public men be appointed to study this question. The facts are all obtainable from the bureau; the department is excellently staffed and the information is available which will enable a commission composed of such men, as I suggested last year, to solve this problem. I leave that suggestion with the minister.

speechtext:
Speaking
personally, and not for the government, I do not think a commission would be able to gather any more facts than are being collected now with respect to transportation. The hon. member suggests that a duty should be placed against the foreign article, but it would not be necessary to appoint a commission to decide that; that would be a matter of policy. Personally, I have always felt that the manufacturers, as well as the domestic users of Ontario, were entitled to receive their coal, which is such an important factor in manufacturing as well as in domestic heating, at as reasonable a price as it could be procured; I do not think it would be fair to ask them to pay any more than they are paying at present. My endeavour has been to supply those consumers with the Canadian product at a price as near as possible to the price they are now paying. Otherwise they would be handicapped to some extent, and I do not think that would be fair. If a contribution is to be made, it should come from the federal government, but so far as I am concerned I do not think there is any necessity to appoint a commission at the moment. We are conducting test movements from both the east and the west in order to establish what is the actual cost of transportation. These movements are not being conducted to determine whether there shall be a dollar, two dollar or three dollar rate, but to establish the actual cost of transportation.

The minister talks about test movements and giving cheap fuel to the Ontario manufacturer, but the fact of the matter is that the coal producers have a protection of about 10 per cent, while some of the Ontario users of coal brought in from the United States have a protection of from 25 to 30 per cent. Is one class of producers not entitled to as adequate protection as another? The minister referred to some of his young men having been taken away by industrial firms and I am very glad that some of them have found useful employment which they certainly could not find when they were in

the minister's department. The minister made reference to the fuel policy of the government as it concerns coal and coking ovens, but he was unable to answer the question as to whether or not any bounty has been paid. The fact of the matter is that the only installation able to comply with the conditions of that policy is one consisting of ten or fifteen coking ovens which were built in Halifax to replace an old gas plant which had been in existence from time out of mind. I think this plant has been completed, but when it is in operation it will not amount to a row of pins as a commercial unit, and the minister knows that is so.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: The hon. member is aware of the fact that they were using American coal in the old beehive ovens.

It was not a beehive
oven plant. Why are they using American coal in Montreal? If the policy inaugurated by the government was a reasonable one, a _ workable one, why was this large coking plant which has been erected on the bank of the Welland canal not built in the east end of Montreal so that Canadian coal could have been used? It was built at the Welland canal where Nova Scotia coal can get to it only by two ways, either by rail or by being lightered up at a cost almost as great as that of bringing it from Sydney to Montreal. The fact of the matter is that the legislation was of no value; it was known to be no good and it has proved to be just as valuable as we said it would be. It was simply a gesture and nothing more than that.
The minister said that one difficulty and a great one was the matter of sulphur. I state that that difficulty is not at all insuperable. All the sulphur oould be removed out of the gases for a cost of a good deal less than twenty-five cents per tan. All this talk about high sulphur content is only using camouflage to hide behind, nothing more and nothing less.
Some reference was made to the $6.75 rate from Alberta. Coal coming from Alberta to Ontario travels about 2,000 miles. We in Nova Scotia were given a flat rate of $3. If we were given a rate proportionate to the mileage, as we were entitled to, we would have a rate from Sprinighiill, not oif $3 as now, but of $1.80; from M-imto. a rate of $1.60 and from StelLamton a rate of $2.20 instead of S3. I want to tell the minister that about twenty years ago a considerable quantity of Nova Scotia coal was carried to Montreal at a rate of $1.80 from S tell art on. During the years when if was so carried during the win-

ter at that rate, we had surpluses on the Intercolonial. I will admit that it costs more to operate the railway to-day than iit did sixteen years ago, because that is about the time the movement to which I refer took place, but the cost has not increased so much as to change a profitable $1.80 rate to a losing $2 rate. Why should the government apply a blanket rate over the whole of the mari-times, where there is a difference between Minto, the nearest point, and Sydney the furthest, of nearly 400 miles, or practically four-tenths of the whole mileage?
The minister made some reference to the efforts of himself and his department to further the use of Nova Scotia coal in the Montreal district. Unless the minister is greatly belied, on his return from that very enjoyable trip to Germany I understand he was royally entertained in London and he there took the opportunity of suggesting to the people of Great Britain that they were neglecting the market in the St. Lawrence. He suggested that it was a market to which they ought bo pay more attention. I do not think that is quite within his province as Minister of Mines. Still to-night he talks about the great efforts of his department to further the use of Nova Scotia coal in the St. Lawrence valley.
Last winter a considerable quantity of soviet coal entered Canada, and the minister and the government said they were powerless to do anything whatever to prevent such coal from coming in. What was the attitude of the United States in that connection? The first cargo that came into Canada went in the first place to New York. How was it met there? Under the United States system of tariff and under the power given to their president, they were able to deal with it. That coal could not be landed in the United States. The cargo then left New York and travelled all the way around Nova Scotia up the gulf and came into Montreal. Other car-gees followed into Portland thence by rail to Montreal, and this government sat absolutely supine, unable or refusing to do anything to protect the coal industries of Nova Sootia and Alberta, and allowing soviet coal to travel about 6,000 miles, one-third of the circumference of the earth, and enter Canada in free competition with our own coal. The minister did nothing to protect either his friends in the old country or his friends in Nova Scotia or his friends in Alberta in that regard and he has to-day nothing that he can say in defence of his action or lack of action-I leave it to him.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
May I say
in answer to my hon. friend that the only coal that came in from soviet Russia, and a very small quantity at that, was anthracite coal?
I know it was anthracite coal and tihe quantity was considerable.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: With regard to my hon. friend's strictures about my suggesting inter-empire trade in anthracite coal and that alone, this was merely a suggestion on my part that instead of the United States getting the business in anthracite, this trade might well go to Great Britain. I was not interfering for a moment with our own domestic fuel supply, because my hon. friend knows full well that we have no anthracite coal.

I absolutely deny that.
What did it displace ? What have we been endeavouring to displace for the last ten years? We have been trying to displace British anthracite and United States anthracite with domestic coke and if the minister would give us a chance we would do it. That is the answer. The minister should get a better story than that or else remain silent.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: There is a plant in Montreal now and my hon. friend can take advantage of the bonus offered by the government. Let him ship coal and have it used in the Montreal plant, and supplant anthracite. That was the purpose for which the bonus was offered.

The government is allowing German and British coke and tens of thousands of tons of United States coke to enter Canada simply because they will not protect Canadian coke by a duty on coke coming into this country.

Will the hon. member's
leader make a declaration in favour of protection on coke or coal?

What was it my hon.
friend said? I did not hear.

Certainly; on both.
